In my country, they say you dont buy a home for yourself, you buy a home for your children. The rationale behind that statement is that by the time most people finish paying their home off, they usually only have a few years left to enjoy it mortgage free. The ones who really benefit from the purchase are their children who inherit the already paid for house. 


Many of my high school friends now own and live in the homes they inherited.  (We are of that age where many of our parents have already passed). My parents (who are still around, by the way) did not purchase a house, so there was nothing for me to inherited, so now I'm doing it so my children would be more comfortable in their future. I'm 13 years into a 25 year mortgage. 


Before the mortgage i rented an apartment for one year. I remember chatting with a neighbour there. She mentioned she intended to rent until she died. She said she has no kids and doesn't intend to have any so there would be no one to leave a home to.

replies.author: @stevegooch3709
replies.text: One of the problems with owning a home for many people is that they got locked into a low interest rate. I know that sounds counterintuitive but in general terms mortgages have what is called interest rate path dependency, meaning that when people finance or refinance, they are not able to sell and buy another home at a comparable interest rate (think if you bought 15 years ago and want to buy today). As a result, you can't make a rational decision to sell and therefore are 'stuck' with an existing mortgage or a home you can't sell. It sounds like a good position to be in, but it is not if you want crystalize equity gains and move on. So if I have a mortgage that is, say 15 years old when UST ten year was at 2 percent, what incentive do I have now to sell my home when 30 year mortgages are at 6.5 percent? None. That is part of the reason new home sales have been slacking for the last ten years.

Yeah taxes and definitely home owners insurance have skyrocketed, but I’m still paying way less than my renter friends, and I never have to worry about a landlord kicking me out. 

I’ll also admit that I bought and refinanced at a very fortunate time. My $750 a month for mortgage (insurance and taxes included) is impossible for new homeowners to achieve today. I hope young people get the same opportunity someday that I had 10 years ago.

comments.text:
The bit about interest in loans being frontloaded, so you're not creating much equity misses at least two points:  (1) rent in the areas I lived in was about the same as a mortgage for like houses, so even if you're only banking single-digit thousands of dollars of equity, that is still single-digit thousands of dollars more than you'd be generating with rent and (2) market value increases.  People don't generate wealth simply by the equity in principle they're paying on their loan, they generate wealth because the $400,000 house they bought in 2018 sells for $550,000 in 2025.  And, yes, you need to stay in your house for 5+ years to realize these benefits.

You give up both of those significant paths to wealth when you rent.  I think it would be really sad to be 65, still renting, and owning nothing ... with nothing to show for the last 40 years of paying rent.  Ugh.

comments.text: It may not be the right time for some of these people to buy a house, but at the end of the day, buying a house is the smartest decision anybody can make. Because at some point you stop paying on that mortgage and then you're just responsible for property taxes and insurance, which a landlord is also paying and will include in the rent payment along with everything else maintenance,  repairs etc. So there is no question owning is the best way to go. Also, you can never be evicted from your own house unless you stop paying the mortgage.

comments.author: @ronia3181
comments.text:
I bought my house and have zero regrets.  BUT... I bought it in 2008, the last time the market crashed.  I also did a ton of research and followed the 3 best pieces of advice for buying a home.  1. Buy the smallest house in the nicest neighborhood that you can afford.  2. You can only afford 2X's your gross income.  3. Figure out what you actually need aka you do not need 4 bedrooms when your single, and buy that.   

Also; if you're thinking about buying a home because it's cheaper than renting.  Not at first it isn't.  On a 30 yr mortgage, the first 10 years are going to be more expensive than renting, the next 10 are about the same.  Not until your 20 years in is it going to be cheaper.

comments.author: @yusee2010
comments.text: I never had the luck to have family inheritance but I would say right now I'm living pretty comfortably because of the house sales I had in the past (by no means that I am rich, I only owned where i lived in, no rental properties because i hate being part of the greedy people who control the rental markets even though i understand how it works and how it would make my life easier and reach my financial goals faster). At the end of the day, you really need to look at the big pictures and do researches before making these decisions. I roll my eyes whenever people are telling me that renting better than buying because from a financial perspective, that's not the case. You could use your home equity for a lot of things in the future like investing, home improvements as long as you make wise decisions with those money. I think buying vs renting suit different life goals and at the end of the day you really need make sure you have emergency funds.  A lot of people think that "i have $30k saved up now so I should be buying a $600k house now!" which the mindset leads them being house poor. ALWAYS live below your means and ALWAYS be prepared. Even if you're told that you could afford a house up to $600k, probably just target $450-500k to be on the safe side so when your washer broke, you won't cry about having to pay $300 for someone else to fix it. Don't spend most of your pay cheque towards your house expenses without being able to save any money. I wish the schools teach kids how to manage money and make better financial decisions. Always be mindful and do your own research don't listen to everything people tell you.
